# Kañcanakkhandhajātaka (Ja 56)

**ID:** Ja 56
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kañcanakkhandhajātaka* (Ja 56) is a birth story set in Sāvatthi concerning a newly ordained monk who feels overwhelmed by the extensive categories of moral rules taught to him, including the Ten Precepts, the Short, Medium, and Long Moralities, sense-restraint, and the Pātimokkha [Fausböll 1877]. Convinced that he cannot fulfill these numerous requirements, he resolves to disrobe and return to household life to make merit as a layman, but his teachers escort him to the Buddha [Silk 1994]. The Buddha clarifies the practice by instructing him to focus purely on guarding his bodily, verbal, and mental actions, through which the monk subsequently attains arahantship (*arahattanikūtena desanaṁ niṭṭhapetvā*) [Silk 1994; Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha declares that he himself was the man who found the mass of gold (*kañcanakkhandha*) [Fausböll 1877].
